questions.q: What is the primary goal of penetration testing?
questions.why: Penetration testing simulates real attacks, finding vulnerabilities and exploiting them to demonstrate actual risk. Software development, traffic monitoring, and data recovery are separate activities.

questions.q: Which of the following tools is commonly used for network scanning?
questions.why: Nmap is the standard tool for discovering hosts, open ports, and services on a network. Metasploit is for exploitation, Wireshark for packet analysis, and Nessus for vulnerability scanning.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a vulnerability assessment in penetration testing?
choices: To identify and classify vulnerabilities in systems
questions.why: A vulnerability assessment finds and classifies weaknesses so they can be prioritized, but it stops short of exploiting them. Exploitation is what distinguishes a full penetration test.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a black box penetration test?
choices: The tester has full knowledge of the system
The tester has no prior knowledge of the system
The tester has limited knowledge of the system
The tester has access to the source code
questions.why: In a black box test the tester starts with no inside knowledge, mimicking an external attacker. Full knowledge describes white box testing and limited knowledge describes gray box.

questions.q: Which tool is primarily used for web application security testing?
questions.why: Burp Suite intercepts and manipulates HTTP traffic, making it the go-to tool for web application testing. Nmap scans networks, Metasploit delivers exploits, and Aircrack-ng targets Wi-Fi.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Metasploit Framework in penetration testing?
questions.why: Metasploit is an exploitation framework used to build, customize, and launch exploits and payloads against targets. It is not a traffic monitor, malware analyzer, or backup tool.

questions.q: Which of the following is a method used to bypass authentication mechanisms?
questions.why: A SQL injection payload can trick a login query into always returning true, defeating the authentication mechanism directly. Phishing and social engineering steal credentials instead of bypassing the mechanism itself.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a 'white box' penetration test?
choices: The tester has no knowledge of the system
The tester has partial knowledge of the system
The tester has full knowledge of the system
The tester uses automated tools only
questions.why: White box testing gives the tester full knowledge, often including source code and architecture, allowing the deepest coverage. No knowledge is black box and partial knowledge is gray box.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of privilege escalation?
choices: Exploiting a buffer overflow vulnerability to gain root access
Scanning a network for open ports
questions.why: Privilege escalation means turning limited access into higher authority, such as exploiting a buffer overflow to gain root. Phishing and port scanning are ways of gaining initial access or information.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a penetration testing report?
choices: To document vulnerabilities and recommend remediation
questions.why: The report is the engagement's key deliverable: it documents each vulnerability, its severity, and how to fix it. Continuous monitoring and patch installation are follow-up work done by the client.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a gray box penetration test?
choices: The tester has full access to the system
The tester has no access to the system
The tester has limited knowledge and access to the system
The tester only performs social engineering
questions.why: Gray box testing sits between black and white box: the tester receives partial knowledge or limited credentials, like an insider with basic access. Full or zero access describes the other test types.

questions.q: Which tool is commonly used for wireless network penetration testing?
questions.why: Aircrack-ng is a suite for capturing wireless traffic and cracking Wi-Fi encryption keys. Nmap scans networks, Burp Suite tests web applications, and Nikto scans web servers.

questions.q: Which type of attack is typically tested using a DNS spoofing tool?
questions.why: DNS spoofing redirects victims to attacker-controlled servers, placing the attacker between the user and the real destination. That interception of traffic is the definition of a man-in-the-middle attack.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of social engineering in penetration testing?
choices: To trick users into revealing sensitive information
questions.why: Social engineering tests the human element by tricking users into revealing information or granting access. Firewalls and software flaws are technical targets addressed by other testing methods.

questions.q: What is the primary objective of reconnaissance in penetration testing?
choices: To gather information about the target
questions.why: Reconnaissance is the first phase of a test, quietly gathering information about the target's systems, people, and footprint. Exploitation and payload delivery happen in later phases.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a client-side attack?
questions.why: XSS executes malicious script inside the victim's browser, making it a client-side attack. Buffer overflows, SQL injection, and directory traversal all target the server side.

questions.q: Which tool is typically used for brute force password attacks?
questions.why: Hydra is purpose-built for fast, automated password guessing against many login services. Nmap scans networks, Metasploit delivers exploits, and Burp Suite focuses on web application testing.

questions.q: Which of the following is a method used to obfuscate code in penetration testing?
questions.why: Encoding, such as Base64, transforms code into another representation to hide its intent while staying reversible without a key. Hashing is one-way, and compression and steganography serve other purposes, so encoding is the obfuscation choice here.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common technique for evading IDS/IPS during penetration testing?
questions.why: Splitting malicious traffic into small fragments can prevent an IDS/IPS from reassembling and matching the attack signature. The other options are attacks in their own right, not evasion techniques.

questions.q: Which of the following is a critical element of a penetration test plan?
questions.why: A test plan must define scope, starting with which target systems are in bounds. Writing exploits happens during the test itself, and performance monitoring and data recovery are not pen test tasks.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common post-exploitation task?
questions.why: After gaining access, testers demonstrate impact through tasks like exfiltrating data. Vulnerability scanning and social engineering happen earlier in the engagement, before exploitation.

questions.q: What is the purpose of privilege escalation in penetration testing?
choices: To gain unauthorized access to higher levels of authority
questions.why: Privilege escalation moves an attacker from a low-privilege foothold to administrator or root authority, unlocking more of the system. Scanning, file recovery, and monitoring are unrelated goals.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary concern when conducting a physical penetration test?
choices: Avoiding detection by physical security measures
questions.why: Physical pen tests attempt to enter facilities, so evading guards, cameras, and locks without being detected is the central challenge. Exploit development and malware analysis are digital tasks.

questions.q: Which type of attack involves injecting malicious SQL queries into a database?
questions.why: SQL injection inserts malicious SQL through input fields so the database executes the attacker's queries. XSS targets browsers, buffer overflows target memory, and DNS spoofing targets name resolution.

questions.q: Which tool is primarily used for network protocol analysis?
questions.why: Wireshark captures packets and decodes hundreds of protocols in detail, making it the standard protocol analyzer. Nmap scans hosts, Metasploit delivers exploits, and Burp Suite tests web applications.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a social engineering attack?
choices: Gaining unauthorized access by exploiting a software vulnerability
Tricking users into revealing confidential information
Intercepting and altering communications between two parties
questions.why: Social engineering manipulates people into giving up confidential information. Exploiting software flaws, intercepting communications, and disguising malware are technical attack techniques.

questions.q: Which of the following is an effective countermeasure against brute force attacks?
questions.why: Account lockout policies block further attempts after a set number of failed logins, defeating the trial-and-error approach brute force depends on. Weak passwords and disabled encryption help attackers.

questions.q: Which tool is commonly used for automated vulnerability scanning?
questions.why: Nessus is a dedicated scanner that automatically checks systems against a large database of known vulnerabilities. Nmap maps networks, Metasploit exploits targets, and Wireshark analyzes packets.

questions.q: Which of the following is a method of data exfiltration during a penetration test?
questions.why: Sending stolen data out through an encrypted tunnel hides it from network monitoring, a classic exfiltration technique. Sniffing, injection, and brute force are ways to gain data or access, not to smuggle it out.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common method used to evade detection by antivirus software?
questions.why: Obfuscating code changes its appearance so signature-based antivirus no longer recognizes it. Phishing and social engineering target people, and SQL injection targets databases, not antivirus detection.

questions.q: What is the primary goal of a penetration testing report?
choices: To document findings and provide recommendations
questions.why: The report documents every finding, rates its severity, and gives the client concrete remediation recommendations. Monitoring, encryption, and exploit development are not the report's purpose.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a gray box penetration test?
choices: The tester has no access to the system
The tester has full access to the system
The tester has limited knowledge and access to the system
The tester only performs network scanning
questions.why: Gray box testing gives the tester partial knowledge and limited access, simulating an insider or partially informed attacker. Full access is white box and no access is black box.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary objective of reconnaissance in penetration testing?
choices: To gather information about the target
questions.why: Reconnaissance means collecting information about the target, such as domains, hosts, and employees, before attacking. Exploitation and malware deployment come later in the process.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a black box penetration test?
choices: The tester has full knowledge of the system
The tester has no prior knowledge of the system
The tester has partial knowledge of the system
The tester has access to the source code
questions.why: Black box testing starts with zero inside knowledge, simulating an external attacker who must discover everything from scratch. Full or partial knowledge describes white box and gray box tests.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the Metasploit Framework in penetration testing?
questions.why: Metasploit exists to develop and deliver exploits and payloads against vulnerable targets. Traffic monitoring, malware analysis, and backups are handled by other tools entirely.

questions.q: During scoping, what does a Rules of Engagement (RoE) document primarily establish?
choices: The permitted targets, methods, timing, and communication procedures
The exact vulnerabilities the tester expects to find
The programming languages used to write the exploits
The antivirus products installed on the target hosts
questions.why: Rules of Engagement define what is in scope, which techniques are allowed, the testing window, and escalation contacts, setting the legal and operational boundaries.

questions.q: Why should a tester carry a signed authorization letter, sometimes called a get-out-of-jail card, during an on-site engagement?
choices: It proves the activity is authorized if the tester is stopped or detained
It guarantees the tester will locate critical vulnerabilities
It exempts the client from paying for remediation
It legally permits bypassing every physical lock on site
questions.why: The authorization letter shows a responsible party approved the work, protecting the tester if security staff or police intervene during physical testing.

questions.q: Before testing an application hosted on a third-party cloud platform, why might extra authorization be required?
choices: The provider owns the shared infrastructure and sets its own testing rules
Cloud applications cannot be tested with any standard tooling
The tester must first purchase a subscription to the platform
Encryption in the cloud makes all such testing illegal
questions.why: Providers own shared infrastructure, so scanning or exploiting hosted assets may breach their acceptable use policy unless their testing terms are followed.

questions.q: A Statement of Work (SOW) agreed before testing chiefly documents which of these?
choices: The deliverables, timeline, and scope of the engagement
The precise vulnerabilities that will be discovered
The internal passwords used by the client
The signatures of every employee at the client
questions.why: The SOW formalizes objectives, scope, schedule, and deliverables so both parties share clear expectations before any work begins.

questions.q: An enumeration scan finds UDP port 161 open with the default community string 'public'. What can a tester likely retrieve?
choices: System configuration and device details through SNMP queries
A full copy of the server's hard drive
The cleartext session keys of every HTTPS connection
questions.why: A readable SNMP community string exposes interface tables, running processes, routing data, and other device details useful for mapping the target.

questions.q: The enum4linux tool run against a Windows host is most useful for extracting what over SMB?
choices: User accounts, groups, and shares via null or authenticated sessions
Wireless pre-shared keys stored on disk
The private keys backing the TLS certificate
questions.why: enum4linux queries SMB and RPC to list users, groups, password policy, and shares, often through null sessions, feeding later password attacks.

questions.q: A tester connects to port 389 and performs an anonymous bind that returns directory objects. What does this reveal?
choices: The LDAP server permits unauthenticated queries of directory data
The domain controller has already been fully compromised
The tester has obtained domain administrator rights
The server is actually a honeypot
questions.why: An anonymous bind that returns results means LDAP exposes directory information without credentials, disclosing users, groups, and organizational structure.

questions.q: A successful AXFR request to a DNS server provides a tester with what?
choices: A complete list of DNS records for the zone
Administrative access to the DNS server itself
The name server's root password hash
An interactive reverse shell on the name server
questions.why: An unrestricted zone transfer dumps every record in the zone, mapping hostnames and addresses that accelerate target discovery.

questions.q: Forcing a web server to fetch a URL the tester supplies, such as an internal cloud metadata endpoint, is characteristic of which flaw?
questions.why: SSRF abuses server-side URL fetching to reach internal services or metadata endpoints that the attacker could not otherwise contact directly.

questions.q: An application accepts a serialized object from the client and rebuilds it without validation. What is the main danger?
choices: Insecure deserialization that can lead to remote code execution
A broken CSS layout on the page
questions.why: Deserializing attacker-controlled data can instantiate malicious objects or gadget chains, frequently resulting in remote code execution.

questions.q: Submitting XML that declares an external entity pointing to /etc/passwd targets which vulnerability class?
questions.why: A parser that resolves external entities can be coerced into reading local files or making outbound requests, which is the core of an XXE attack.

questions.q: Capturing a victim's NTLM authentication and forwarding it to another service to authenticate as that user describes what attack?
questions.why: An NTLM relay forwards captured authentication to a third host, gaining access as the victim without ever cracking the underlying password.

questions.q: Requesting service tickets for accounts that have a Service Principal Name and cracking them offline is known as what?
questions.why: Kerberoasting requests TGS tickets for service accounts, whose encrypted portion can be cracked offline to recover the service account password.

questions.q: To crack WPA2-PSK, capturing which piece of data enables an offline dictionary attack?
choices: The 4-way handshake or an exposed PMKID
The access point's MAC vendor prefix
questions.why: The WPA2 4-way handshake, or an exposed PMKID, contains material that lets a tester brute force the passphrase offline without touching the AP again.

questions.q: Standing up a rogue access point that copies a legitimate SSID to lure clients is called what?
questions.why: An evil twin mimics a trusted SSID so clients connect to the attacker's access point, enabling traffic interception and credential capture.

questions.q: On Windows, a service whose executable path contains spaces and is unquoted can enable escalation because Windows may do what?
choices: Execute a malicious binary planted earlier in the path
Reveal the entire SAM database automatically
Grant the Guest account administrator rights
questions.why: With an unquoted path containing spaces, Windows tries each fragment, so a writable earlier directory lets an attacker plant a binary run as the service account.

questions.q: A Linux SUID-root binary that can spawn a shell, as catalogued by GTFOBins, is dangerous because a low-privilege user can do what?
choices: Run commands with the file owner's root privileges
questions.why: A SUID binary executes as its owner, so if it is root-owned and abusable it can be leveraged to run commands as root and escalate privileges.

questions.q: During Linux escalation, running 'sudo -l' is useful mainly to reveal what?
choices: Which commands the current user may run as another user
The exact kernel version and patch level
Every open network socket on the host
questions.why: sudo -l lists the user's permitted sudo commands, exposing misconfigurations such as NOPASSWD entries that open a path to privilege escalation.

questions.q: After compromising a dual-homed host, using SSH dynamic port forwarding with proxychains lets a tester accomplish what?
choices: Route tools through the compromised host to reach an internal network
questions.why: SSH dynamic forwarding opens a SOCKS proxy on the pivot host, so tools run through proxychains can reach systems routable only from that machine.

questions.q: The Metasploit autoroute module is used after gaining a session to achieve what?
choices: Pivot traffic to subnets reachable only through the compromised host
Encrypt the Meterpreter payload in transit
questions.why: autoroute adds routes through an existing session so other Metasploit modules can target internal subnets reachable from the initial foothold.

questions.q: A WAF blocks the string 'UNION SELECT'. Alternating case, inline comments, or URL encoding are attempts to do what?
choices: Fix a syntax error in the payload
questions.why: Obfuscating a payload with case changes, comments, or encoding aims to evade the WAF's pattern signatures while the database still interprets it correctly.

questions.q: Tunneling command-and-control traffic over HTTPS to a trusted CDN domain helps an operator evade defenses by doing what?
choices: Blending C2 traffic in with legitimate encrypted web traffic
Disabling the target's TLS inspection hardware
Removing the need for any C2 listener
questions.why: Routing C2 through HTTPS to reputable domains makes malicious traffic resemble normal browsing, complicating detection and network blocking.

questions.q: Configuring Nmap with a very slow timing template such as -T0 or -T1 is intended to do what?
choices: Reduce the chance that rate-based IDS thresholds trigger an alert
Scan every port on the host in under a second
Remove the need for prior authorization
questions.why: Slower timing spreads probes out so scan-detection thresholds based on traffic rate are less likely to fire, at the cost of a much longer scan.

questions.q: Running Mimikatz against the LSASS process on a compromised Windows host is typically done to obtain what?
choices: Cached credentials and NTLM hashes from memory
questions.why: LSASS holds authentication material, so dumping it with Mimikatz can yield plaintext passwords, hashes, or tickets used for lateral movement.

questions.q: Adding a Windows registry Run key entry or creating a scheduled task after exploitation serves which post-exploitation goal?
choices: Maintaining persistence across reboots and logins
Escalating instantly from user to SYSTEM
Encrypting the attacker's payload on disk
questions.why: Run keys and scheduled tasks relaunch the attacker's payload automatically, preserving access after the host restarts or the user logs off.

questions.q: Authenticating to a remote Windows service using a captured NTLM hash, without the plaintext password, is called what?
questions.why: Pass-the-hash reuses the NTLM hash directly in the challenge-response exchange, so no cracking is needed to authenticate as the compromised user.

questions.q: In a penetration test report, the executive summary should be written primarily for whom?
choices: Business leaders who need risk and impact in non-technical terms
Developers who need copy-paste exploit code
Only the IDS signature tuning team
questions.why: The executive summary conveys overall risk, business impact, and priorities to management, while deep technical detail lives in the findings section.

questions.q: The CVSS base score included in a report conveys what about each finding?
choices: A standardized, vendor-neutral measure of technical severity
The exact dollar cost of remediation
questions.why: CVSS gives a repeatable severity rating derived from exploitability and impact metrics, helping clients compare and prioritize findings consistently.

questions.q: When assigning a risk rating to a finding, testers commonly combine impact with which other factor?
choices: The likelihood the vulnerability will actually be exploited
The number of pages in the final report
The tester's total years of experience
The color scheme of the reporting dashboard
questions.why: Risk is generally impact multiplied by likelihood, so a severe but hard-to-exploit issue may rank below an easily exploited moderate one.

questions.q: After the client remediates reported issues, why is a retest or validation phase valuable?
choices: It confirms fixes work and did not introduce new gaps
It automatically renews the tester's certification
It deletes the original report for confidentiality
It removes the need for a scope agreement
questions.why: Retesting verifies that remediation actually closed each vulnerability and did not create new weaknesses, properly closing out the engagement.
